2026.9 TDL TREND REPORT

Pallet Storage Systems

What products will you store,
and how much capacity do you need?

From manual racking to stacker cranes and shuttles
Selecting storage systems by density, investment, SKU flexibility and storage volume

05 TYPESManual Storage Systems
03 TYPESAutomated System Types
CH.1

Three Criteria for Evaluating Storage Systems

This report examines where pallets are stored, at what density and how they are picked. System selection should consider not only storage capacity, but also the SKU mix and outbound flow during peak periods.

01 · DENSITY

Storage Density

The number of pallet positions achieved within the same floor area. Compare aisle width, lane depth and storage height together.

02 · COST

Investment

The relative investment required for racking, handling equipment, controls and installation. A “High” rating means a higher cost burden.

03 · USABILITY

Suitability

Two dimensions are evaluated separately: flexibility across many SKUs and suitability for large inventory volumes. Throughput must be validated as a separate design requirement.

MANUAL

Operator-driven forklifts put pallets into and retrieve them from the racking.
Selective pallet racking / VNA high-bay racking / Pallet flow racking / Drive-in racking / Push-back racking

AUTOMATED

Stacker cranes, two-way shuttles and four-way shuttles automate pallet storage and picking. Each system uses a different method for I/O handoff and movement between levels and lanes.
Stacker crane / Two-way shuttle / Four-way shuttle

Terminology used in this issue: “Storage density” refers to storage positions per unit of floor area, not current inventory occupancy. “High-bay” describes height and “VNA” describes a very narrow aisle; this report covers VNA high-bay racking operated with a turret truck.
CH.2

Manual Storage Systems · 5 Types

Select a system to review how it works and the conditions it requires. Pallet flow and push-back racks use gravity to move loads, while putaway and picking are performed by operator-driven forklifts in the configurations covered here.

SELECTIVE PALLET RACK

The standard system for direct pallet access

Forklifts place and retrieve pallets from racks built with uprights and horizontal beams. This report uses single-deep selective pallet racking as the reference configuration. Direct access to every pallet makes it a strong baseline for warehouses with many SKUs and low stock per SKU.

Best Fit
Many SKUs / Low volume per SKU / Frequent individual picks

01Forklift transfers through the aisle
02Place the pallet in its assigned position
03Directly pick the required pallet

Advantages

  • Direct access: Retrieve the required pallet without moving another pallet first.
  • Flexible layout: Beam levels and bays can be configured to match load dimensions.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Aisle footprint: Forklift operating aisles reduce the floor area available for storage.
  • Load conditions: Verify pallet and beam loads, load overhang and impact protection.
  • Inventory sequence: FIFO is achieved through location control and work instructions, not by the rack itself.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Pallet Racking ↗

HIGH-BAY / VERY NARROW AISLE

Narrower aisles with greater use of height

High pallet racking is combined with very narrow aisles and served by dedicated VNA turret trucks. High-bay describes height, while VNA describes aisle width; the terms are not exact synonyms. This report covers operator-driven VNA operations.

Best Fit
High clear height / Many palletized SKUs / Limited floor area

01Turret truck enters the aisle
02Raise and rotate the forks
03High-bay pallet storage and retrieval

Advantages

  • Space use: Narrow aisles and greater storage height increase usable capacity.
  • Selectivity: A single-deep layout preserves direct access to each pallet.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Floor and guidance: Check floor flatness and rail- or wire-guidance requirements.
  • Dedicated equipment: The system cannot be planned around standard forklifts.
  • Overall traffic: Design transfer space at aisle entrances and replenishment traffic together.

Operating principle reference: Jungheinrich · EKX 410–516 ↗

DRIVE-IN RACK

High-density storage with forklifts entering the rack

A forklift enters between pallet-support rails and stores pallets from the back forward. Eliminating intermediate aisles enables deep storage of the same SKU. Single-entry drive-in racking normally follows LIFO; drive-through racking with access from both sides is different.

LIFO (Last In, First Out): Inventory received last is picked first.

Best Fit
Few SKUs / High volume / Lot-based operation / LIFO acceptable

01Forklift enters the lane
02Store pallets from the back
03Pick the pallet nearest the entrance

Advantages

  • Dense storage: Reduce operating aisles and store pallets deeper within the same area.
  • Simple structure: Achieve dense storage without shuttle or crane drives.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Access limitation: Pallets at the front may block retrieval of pallets stored deeper in the lane.
  • Impact control: Forklifts enter the rack, making operating clearance and protection critical.
  • Effective occupancy: Separating lanes by SKU and lot can leave unused positions.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Drive-In Racking ↗

PUSH-BACK RACK

Load by pushing back and retrieve from the front

As a forklift loads a new pallet, existing pallets are pushed back on inclined carts or rollers. When the front pallet is removed, the remaining loads roll forward by gravity. Putaway and picking from the same face create a LIFO flow.

LIFO (Last In, First Out): Inventory received last is picked first.

Best Fit
Multiple pallets per SKU / Single-face operation / LIFO acceptable

01Push existing loads back with a new pallet
02Accumulate pallets toward the rear
03Remaining loads advance after the front pallet is picked

Advantages

  • No rack entry: The forklift operates from the aisle.
  • Lane-based operation: SKUs can be assigned by level and lane for dense storage.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Picking sequence: May not suit inventory requiring strict FIFO.
  • Pallet compatibility: Verify compatibility between pallet bottoms and carts or rollers.
  • Controlled movement: Validate speed and impact as loads are pushed back and return forward.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Push-Back Racking ↗

PALLET FLOW RACK

Gravity-fed first-in, first-out storage

Pallets loaded onto inclined roller lanes move toward the picking side by gravity. A typical FIFO configuration uses putaway at the higher end and picking at the opposite, lower end. Loads move by themselves, but forklifts perform putaway and picking, so the system is classified here as manual.

FIFO (First In, First Out): Inventory received first is picked first.

Best Fit
High volume per SKU / Sequential picking / Separate putaway and picking faces

01Load pallets from the putaway side
02Move along inclined rollers
03Pick in sequence from the opposite side

Advantages

  • Inventory flow: The lane naturally supports a first-in, first-out sequence.
  • Separated traffic: Putaway and picking can be performed from different faces.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Physical testing: Validate slope and braking for the pallet base and load weight.
  • Lane assignment: Define how the same SKU and compatible lots will be grouped.
  • Jam response: Define a safe procedure to stop work, clear roller jams or damaged pallets and resume picking.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Pallet Flow Racking ↗

Manual System Comparison

Ratings are qualitative and relative within the manual-system group. “High” investment means a higher cost burden. Suitability describes fit for SKU variety and inventory volume, not handling speed.

Storage Density

Storage density achieved within the same floor area and load dimensions by using aisles, lane depth and height.

Suitability · SKU Variety

How easily one system can separate multiple SKUs and lots and provide access to required inventory.

Suitability · Storage Volume

How well the system accommodates many pallets of the same SKU in deep lanes or at height.

How to Read the Manual-System Ratings

Selective and VNA high-bay racks provide direct pallet access and suit a wide variety of SKUs. Pallet flow, drive-in and push-back systems reduce aisle space and use deeper lanes, improving density and bulk-storage suitability, but lane assignment by SKU and lot lowers SKU flexibility.

Suitability ratings do not represent throughput. Actual throughput must be validated separately using forklift quantity, travel distance, staffing, I/O-face configuration and peak volume.

Manual-system storage height: Storage height is determined by forklift residual capacity and lift height, building clear height and rack structure. Public reference values include a maximum lift height of 18 m for Jungheinrich EKX models and a maximum rack height of 7.5 m for Mecalux push-back racking. Forklift lift height and rack height are different measures and should not be applied as universal maxima.
CH.3

Automated Storage Systems · 3 System Types

Stacker cranes are divided into single- and double-deep configurations. Shuttle systems differ not only by travel direction but also by which equipment handles lane changes, level changes and I/O handoff. The two-way shuttle section assumes forklifts handle putaway, picking and movement between levels and lanes.

Crane aisleFront position

Plan-view concept for one side of an aisle · Not to scale

STACKER CRANE / SINGLE DEEP

High-bay storage with direct pallet access

A stacker crane travels along the rack aisle while its carriage and forks automatically store and retrieve pallets. Single-deep layouts provide one pallet position on each side of the aisle, so no other pallet blocks the target load. This supports individual picking across a broad SKU range.

Best Fit
Many SKUs / Direct pallet access / High-bay automated warehouse

01Handoff from the inbound conveyor
02Crane travel and lift
03Fork putaway or retrieval at the assigned position

Advantages

  • Direct access: No relocation of a front pallet is required.
  • High-bay use: Combines vertical storage with automated position control.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Aisle throughput: Work in each aisle may depend on a single crane.
  • Expansion: More aisles and cranes may be required to increase throughput.
  • Failure impact: With one crane per aisle, a crane failure stops all putaway and retrieval in that aisle. Inventory in the affected aisle cannot be accessed normally until recovery.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Stacker Cranes ↗

Crane aisleFront positionRear position

Plan-view concept for one side of an aisle · Not to scale

STACKER CRANE / DOUBLE DEEP

Two-deep storage for more capacity per aisle

Each side of the aisle is configured two pallets deep and a telescopic fork reaches the rear position. This reduces aisle share versus single-deep storage, but a front pallet may need to be relocated before accessing the rear pallet. Pairing the same SKU or lot is therefore important.

Best Fit
Adequate stock per SKU / Space constraints / Relocation workload acceptable

01Assign the inbound pallet and storage location
02Store in front or rear with a telescopic fork
03Check the front position; relocate if required before picking

Advantages

  • Higher storage efficiency: Reduce aisle share and increase pallet positions versus single-deep storage.
  • Height plus depth: Use vertical space and storage depth together.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Additional moves: Relocating the front pallet for rear picks can reduce effective throughput.
  • Location strategy: Manage long-term isolation of rear pallets and mixed lots.
  • Failure impact: With one crane per aisle, a crane failure stops all putaway and retrieval in that aisle. Inventory in the affected aisle cannot be accessed normally until recovery.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Stacker Cranes ↗

Two-way shuttle concept · Division of work between forklift and shuttle

2-WAY PALLET SHUTTLE / AUTOMATED

Forklift to the lane entrance, shuttle into the lane

The forklift places the pallet and shuttle at the required level and lane entrance. The shuttle then travels forward and backward on rails to carry the pallet to an internal storage position. For outbound handling, the shuttle returns the pallet to the lane entrance and the forklift picks it. The base configuration does not use a lift.

Best Fit
High volume per SKU / Deep lanes / Continued forklift operation

01Forklift places the shuttle and pallet at the lane entrance
02Shuttle travels forward and backward in the lane
03Shuttle returns the pallet; forklift picks it

Advantages

  • Deep lanes: Achieve dense storage without forklifts entering the rack.
  • Division of work: The shuttle handles repeated travel within a lane; the forklift handles lane and level changes.
  • Productivity and issue response: Where multiple shuttles can work in parallel and a spare can replace a failed unit, scaling throughput and responding to individual equipment failures can be easier than with one crane per aisle. Actual throughput remains constrained by forklift capacity.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Forklift dependency: Lane changes, putaway and picking depend on operator and forklift capacity.
  • Shuttle operation: Plan shuttle quantity, lane transfers and charging time together.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · Forklift-Served Pallet Shuttle ↗

4-WAY PALLET SHUTTLE

Autonomous forward, backward and lateral lane travel

The shuttle moves along both horizontal axes to access multiple lanes. In multi-level configurations, lifts provide vertical transfer. Fleet dispatching and route control for multiple shuttles connect storage density with throughput.

Best Fit
Dense storage / Multiple connected lanes / Scalable throughput

01Handoff at the I/O station
02Shuttle travels in four directions
03Use a lift for level changes when required

Advantages

  • Flexible access: The shuttle performs its own horizontal lane changes.
  • Higher productivity: If lifts and intersections have spare capacity, parallel shuttle operation can scale throughput more easily than a one-crane-per-aisle configuration.
  • Issue response: A failed shuttle can be isolated and tasks reassigned to healthy units, reducing the impact of an individual equipment failure. Alternate routes and spare equipment are prerequisites.
  • Higher storage density: Compared with forklift-served two-way shuttles, four-way systems can reduce forklift aisles and connect storage zones to increase capacity within the same building. Cross aisles and lift footprints must be included in the comparison.

Design & Operating Considerations

  • Shared bottlenecks: Saturated lifts or intersections reduce the benefit of adding shuttles.
  • Deep inventory: Four-direction travel does not guarantee direct access to every pallet.
  • Failure scope: A failed shuttle blocking a route, or a fault in a shared lift or control system, can affect multiple lanes or the entire system.

Operating principle reference: Mecalux · 3D Automated Pallet Shuttle ↗

Automated System Comparison

Ratings are qualitative and relative within the automated-system group. Suitability reflects fit for SKU variety and inventory volume; throughput must be calculated separately using equipment quantity and shared-system bottlenecks.

Storage Density

Compare storage density within the same building, including crane aisles, shuttle cross aisles and lift footprints.

Suitability · SKU Variety

How easily the system separates positions by SKU and lot, accesses a target pallet or changes routes.

Suitability · Storage Volume

How well the system accommodates high volumes of the same SKU in deep lanes and at height.

How to Read the Automated-System Ratings

Single-deep systems offer high SKU flexibility through direct pallet access, but crane aisles reduce storage-volume suitability, rated Low. Double-deep systems add positions while automated location control supports multiple SKUs, resulting in Medium storage-volume suitability and High SKU flexibility.

Two-way shuttles suit high volumes of the same SKU in deep lanes. Four-way shuttles move across multiple lanes and handle a broader SKU range, but deep-lane structure and inventory-placement constraints result in a Medium SKU-flexibility rating.

Key Crane and Shuttle Comparisons

01 · STORAGE DENSITY

Single-Deep → Double-Deep

Double-deep storage reduces aisle share and increases density versus single-deep storage. Account for front-pallet relocation when picking rear positions and for empty positions created by SKU and lot separation.

02 · PRODUCTIVITY & RECOVERY

Crane → Multiple Shuttles

Multiple shuttles can work in parallel and substitute for one another, which can improve productivity and response to individual equipment failures versus one crane per aisle. Two-way systems depend on forklift capacity; four-way systems depend on available lift and intersection capacity.

03 · STORAGE DENSITY

Two-Way → Four-Way

A four-way layout can achieve higher storage density than a forklift-served two-way system by reducing operating aisles. Compare effective capacity after including cross aisles and lift footprints.

CH.5

System Selection · Start with Inventory and Peak Volume

Use actual inventory and I/O history by SKU to validate each candidate system’s storage density, investment and suitability.

Four Inputs for System Evaluation

01

Load Characteristics

Check dimensions, overall height, weight, base type and rates of overhang or damage. Define exception handling for nonconforming loads.

02

Inventory Characteristics

Review maximum and average inventory by SKU, as well as lot and expiry requirements. Test lane depths to determine effective capacity.

03

Throughput Characteristics

Account for inbound and outbound volume by time period, concurrent work and order concentration. Do not size equipment from average volume alone.

04

Infrastructure Characteristics

Review clear height, columns, floor conditions, temperature, maintenance access and recovery methods. Compare initial investment and maintenance cost together.

KEY POINT

The key to storage-system selection is securing the right fit for SKU variety and inventory volume while validating the balance between storage density and total operating cost.

CHECK

Check Your Understanding: Five Questions

Terminology: FIFO (First In, First Out) picks the inventory received first; LIFO (Last In, First Out) picks the inventory received last; FEFO (First Expired, First Out) picks the inventory with the earliest expiry date first.
